fields.h1: The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith: Summary and Study Guide
fields.meta_title: Torrey, The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith — Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A reader's study guide to R. A. Torrey's The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith: what the book covers, its central themes, who should read it, how to read it today, and questions for reflection. Free full text on Ochorus.
fields.body_html:
If you have ever sat in a pew and quietly wondered whether you could actually say what you believe — and why — this book was written for you. The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith is R. A. Torrey’s plain, unhurried walk through the great truths every Christian stands on: the Bible, God, Christ, the Holy Spirit, the atonement, salvation, and the things to come. It is short, clear, and thoroughly practical, and Ochorus hosts the whole text free to read. This guide is a companion to help you read it well — a map of what the book is, how it is arranged, what it keeps coming back to, and how to make its teaching your own.

What the book is, and Torrey’s aim

The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith is not a work of technical theology written for the lecture hall. It is a series of sermons Torrey preached to his own congregation, week by week, out of a simple pastoral conviction: that new believers and old alike were vague about what they held and why. He states the problem in his preface without softening it.

We live in a day in which many of our church members are all at sea as to what they believe on the fundamental doctrines of the Christian faith.

R. A. Torrey

His answer to that drift was not novelty but instruction — what he calls systematic teaching in the truths a Christian is meant to know. Torrey was an evangelist and educator associated with D. L. Moody’s work, and his instinct throughout is to ground everything the reader believes in the Bible itself, so that the teaching is not received on his authority but tested against Scripture. He builds each doctrine on cited passages, quotes them at length, and expects the reader to keep a Bible open beside the book. The aim, in short, is to give an ordinary believer a clear, orderly, Bible-anchored grasp of the essentials of the faith — a foundation firm enough to stand on and simple enough to explain to someone else.

How the book is organized

Torrey arranges the doctrines in a deliberate order, and the sequence itself is part of the teaching. He begins where he believes everything else must rest — the inspiration of the Bible — and only then builds upward. The chapters move through the faith like this:

  • The inspiration of the Bible — to what extent Scripture is inspired of God, and why that question decides all the rest (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21).
  • The being and nature of God — the God of the Bible, his infinite perfection and unity, set against the counterfeits of his day (1 John 1:5; 1 John 4:8).
  • The person of Christ — two chapters, one on the deity of Jesus Christ and one on his real and full humanity (John 1:1; John 1:14).
  • The Holy Spirit — his personality, his deity, and his distinction from the Father and the Son.
  • The atonement — God’s doctrine of the cross set over against the denials of it Torrey saw around him.
  • Salvation applied — justification by faith, the new birth, and sanctification (Acts 13:38; John 3:3; 1 Thessalonians 5:23).
  • The things to come — the resurrection of the body, and the sober chapters on the devil, hell, and future punishment (Luke 24:39).

The shape is intentional. Once the Bible is settled as the court of final appeal, Torrey can build doctrine after doctrine on it; and because he moves from God, to Christ, to the Spirit, to salvation, to the last things, the sermons together form a connected whole rather than a set of separate lectures.

Two features of the arrangement are worth noticing before you begin. First, Torrey gives the person of Christ two full chapters rather than one — insisting on both his deity and his real, complete humanity — because he regards a wrong view at either end as fatal to the rest. Second, he does not stop at the comforting doctrines. The closing chapters on the devil, on whether there is a literal hell, and on whether future punishment is everlasting are as plainly and scripturally handled as the chapters on justification and the new birth. Torrey treats them as part of the same body of truth, to be taught rather than avoided, and their sober tone is deliberate.

Central themes

Read straight through, a few convictions surface again and again. The first is that doctrine is not optional furniture for the Christian life but its structure. Torrey is convinced that what you believe about God, Christ, and salvation will shape everything else, and that muddled belief produces muddled living. He is patient with honest questions but firm that the answers matter.

The second theme is the centrality of the person of Christ. For Torrey, the most fundamental question a person can be asked is the one Jesus put to the Pharisees in Matthew 22:42 — what do you think of the Christ? Everything turns on the answer.

If a man really holds right views concerning the person of Jesus Christ he will sooner or later get right views on every other question.

R. A. Torrey

The third is that salvation is God’s work received by faith, not a wage earned by effort. When Torrey reaches justification, he treats it as the truth that made the Reformation and the hinge of the whole gospel, tracing it from Abraham, who believed God and had it counted to him for righteousness (Genesis 15:6), through Paul’s declaration in Romans 4:5.

The doctrine of Justification by Faith was the doctrine that made the Reformation.

R. A. Torrey

Underneath all of it runs the fourth and steadiest theme: the Bible is the foundation. Torrey never asks the reader to take a doctrine because he says so. He shows it in the text, quotes chapter and verse, and hands the reader the means to check him. That method — persuading from the Word rather than from the pulpit’s authority — is the book’s abiding character.

A fifth note runs quietly through the whole: an honest realism about sin and its remedy. Torrey does not present the faith as a set of pleasant ideas. Christ is fully God and truly man because a real Saviour was needed for real guilt; the new birth is necessary, not optional; and the last things are sober because sin is serious. Yet the effect is not gloom but assurance. Because the diagnosis is honest, the good news of justification and regeneration lands as genuinely good — a rescue that has actually been accomplished and can actually be received.

Who should read it

This is a book for the pew, not the seminary, and that is its strength. It will serve, first, any Christian who feels unsure of what they believe or why. If the great doctrines have always seemed like a fog you were expected to have cleared long ago, Torrey walks you through them one at a time, in order, without jargon.

It will serve, second, anyone who teaches or disciples others — a small-group leader, a parent, a new-members class teacher, a pastor looking for a plain scriptural summary to work from. Torrey wrote it hoping other ministers would use it exactly that way, and its clear headings and stacked proof texts make it easy to teach from.

Third, it suits the newer believer being grounded for the first time, and equally the long-time churchgoer who has never quite connected the doctrines into a whole. Because Torrey presents each teaching faithfully and plainly, grounding it in passages the reader can weigh, the book meets both kinds of reader where they are. It is a solid, Bible-based foundation offered to the ordinary Christian — no prior study assumed.

How to read it today

A few practical suggestions will help the book do its work. Read it in order, and start at the beginning. Torrey put inspiration first on purpose; the later chapters lean on it. Working straight through lets the doctrines build the way he intended, so resist the urge to skip to the topic that interests you most.

Keep a Bible open beside you. This is the single most important thing. Torrey means for you to look up the passages, not merely read past them — the point is to see that the teaching rises out of Scripture itself. When he cites John 1:1 for the deity of Christ or Luke 24:39 for the resurrection of the body, turn there and read it in context. The book is designed to make your own Bible the ground of your doctrine.

Take one chapter at a time. Each sermon is a self-contained treatment of one doctrine, well suited to a single sitting or a week’s reflection. Let a chapter settle before you move on. And read it charitably as a document of its era. Torrey often frames a doctrine against the specific errors of his own day, naming the movements he was answering; you can receive the positive teaching he is defending without needing to track every controversy he had in view. Take the truth he is guarding, and let the old arguments serve as the setting rather than the substance.

Finally, read it to be able to tell someone else. Torrey’s whole aim was a church that could say what it believes. A good test of each chapter is whether you could now explain that doctrine simply, with a verse or two, to a friend who asked. If you can, the book has done for you what it set out to do.

For reflection

Use these questions on your own or with a group, a Bible within reach.

  1. Torrey begins with the inspiration of the Bible because everything else rests on it. If Scripture is the court of final appeal, how does that change the way you settle questions of doctrine and duty?
  2. Jesus asks in Matthew 22:42, what do you think of the Christ? How would you answer, and how do John 1:1 and John 1:14 together shape that answer?
  3. Read Romans 4:5 and Genesis 15:6. In your own words, what is the difference between being justified by faith and trying to be justified by your own works?
  4. Which doctrine in the book did you understand least well before reading it — and could you now explain it simply, with a verse, to someone who asked?
  5. Torrey longed for a church no longer “all at sea” about what it believes. Where do you most want to be more firmly grounded, and what would it look like to build that foundation this year?

When you finish, the natural next step is to read Torrey where he goes deeper on a single doctrine. His The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit expands the two chapters here on the Spirit into a full and careful study, and more of his clear, Bible-anchored teaching waits on his author page. The whole of The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith is free to read on Ochorus — a short book, but one that can quietly settle a great deal.
